steps.title: Why treat a stone?
steps.text: A stone taken out of the ground is rarely perfect: a dull colour, cracks, visible inclusions. It can be improved by a treatment. It is legal and common, as long as the buyer is told. A treatment changes the value: a treated stone is generally worth less than an equivalent natural stone, sometimes much less.

steps.title: Changing the colour
steps.text: • Heating: the oldest, and often stable. It lightens or intensifies the colour of ruby, sapphire, tanzanite... • Irradiation (gamma rays, electrons, neutrons): it colours or darkens the stone, for example a blue topaz or a green diamond. • Diffusion: an element (titanium, chromium, beryllium...) is made to enter the surface. It sometimes colours only a tenth of a millimetre. • Dyeing: a porous material (jade, agate, coral, pearl) is coloured with a dye. • Coating: a film of metal or lacquer, like “mystic” topaz or aqua aura.

steps.title: Improving purity and transparency
steps.text: • Filling: oil, wax or resin goes into the cracks and makes them less visible (emerald, ruby, turquoise). A lead glass can fill a heavily cracked ruby. • Laser: the dark inclusion of a diamond is drilled, then bleached with acid. • Bleaching: a bath of hydrogen peroxide or acid lightens pearls, jade and coral. • HPHT: an annealing under high pressure that removes the colour of or lightens some diamonds.

steps.title: Recognizing them
Stable or fragile?
steps.text: Not all treatments are equal. A colour from heating stays. An oil can dry out or run, a melted glass fears heat and acids, a coating wears off. The lesson on stability details what resists or not light, heat and chemicals.

steps.title: To remember
steps.text: • Treating is allowed, but it must be disclosed. • There are colour treatments and purity treatments. • Instruments cross-check their clues to recognize them. • A treatment changes the value and the stability of the stone.
